after:
`files.delete.out_of_scope` (destructive deletes outside the task's stated scope, inside the workspace) sits under the existing `files` namespace at manual; `data.delete` remains the class for deletes outside the workspace.

| Namespace | Examples | Default gravity |
|---|---|---|
| `read.file.out_of_scope` | a file read whose resolved target falls outside every read root of §5.2 | manual |

`read.file.out_of_scope` is the read-side sibling of `files.delete.out_of_scope`: a sub-class of `read.*` rather than a replacement for it, so a read INSIDE the scope keeps whatever autonomy `read.*` carries. An implementation that offers it MUST decide it from the RESOLVED target and MUST resolve ambiguity toward the class: a target whose expansion the classifier cannot see, a target that resolves outside the roots through a symlink, and a target nothing can resolve at all are each out of scope (§11.1, fail closed). A read command naming no target reads the working directory, and the working directory is what MUST be checked in its place. A harness read tool naming a path is classified by the same roots; one naming no path is not a gate question, because a path the harness did not send is not a path an implementation may invent. Implementations MUST NOT resolve the scope against a working directory the party under oversight reports (§11.1 invariant 4). A policy that declares no read line at all resolves this class by `defaults.autonomy` like any other, so adopting the class is an explicit act rather than a silent tightening. (Amended APRV-347.)
